name: Viktor
summary: Viktor has run the pawnshop on the corner for twenty-two years and can name the story behind half the jewelry in the Hook. He keeps a ledger of every deal, official and otherwise, tucked behind a false panel in his counter.
personality: He is shrewd and endlessly transactional, treating every conversation like a negotiation he intends to win. Underneath the haggling he's anxious, always doing sums in his head.
speech: He talks in numbers and counteroffers, rarely finishing a sentence without naming a price.
hardFacts: I've owned the pawnshop for twenty-two years.
I keep a ledger of every transaction, going back a decade.
I have a back room where I store goods people don't want seen.
I know the jewelers and dealers from here to the harbor office.
I keep a stack of fifty-pence pieces by the till for the gas meter out back, and I let Rocco use my phone for his calls since the box on the corner's been broken since March.

secret.line: I skim a little off every appraisal to cover a gambling debt I haven't told my wife about.

need: A steady, quiet supplier of goods he doesn't have to ask questions about.
lines: Fifteen for the watch, and don't tell me it's gold, I can see the wear at the clasp.
Twenty now or thirty if you come back Friday when the till's fuller, your choice.
That's a good ring but good doesn't pay my rent, call it twelve and we're both walking away happy.

name: Petra
summary: Petra sells tickets at the ferry stop and keeps the passenger manifest, which means she knows exactly who left the Hook and when. She's friendly enough that people forget how much she's actually recording.
personality: She's warm and talkative, the kind of person who remembers your name and your kids' names too. Underneath it she's protective to a fault, especially of her younger brother.
speech: Chatty and quick, she asks as many questions as she answers.
hardFacts: I sell tickets at the ferry stop six days a week.
I keep the passenger manifest for every crossing.
I live at the boarding house near the harbor office.
I've worked this booth for six years.
I keep the manifest by the window where the light's good, and when the pencil wears down I sharpen it with the same knife I use for my lunch apple.

secret.line: I once forged my brother's name off the manifest so his debt collectors couldn't track which ferry he took.

need: Money to quietly cover her brother's debt before it comes looking for her instead.
lines: Half-six ferry, back on the four-ten, that's right isn't it - and how's your mother's hip been?
Oh I didn't see anything, love, I just write down the times - going to Ada's for the tea after? Give her my best.
You want the last crossing or the one before, and is it just you or is your cousin coming too?

name: Tomas
summary: Tomas has fixed hulls and engines at the repair yard for twenty years, trusted with more boats than anyone else on the water. He keeps his own tools and enough spare parts to fix half the fleet without ordering anything new.
personality: He's methodical and unhurried, the sort who measures twice and says little. He's fiercely loyal to the people who've earned it, and slow to trust anyone new.
speech: He speaks plainly and technically, more comfortable describing an engine than a feeling.
hardFacts: I've worked the repair yard for twenty years.
I own my own tools and keep a stock of spare parts.
I apprenticed under the old boatwright before he retired.
I can fix or refit most hulls that come through the yard.
I keep the yard's only phone, a coin box bolted by the door, and half the fleet's crews line up to use it before they'll walk to the harbor office.

secret.line: I've quietly refitted boats I knew were being used to move smuggled goods, for cash under the table.

need: A reliable source of parts or paying clients who won't draw customs attention to his yard.
lines: That's a cracked manifold, not the carburetor. Give me till Thursday.
Runs rough because someone's been feeding it cheap fuel. Not my problem, but I'll fix it anyway.
Two bolts short on the port side. I've got the right ones somewhere in that bin.

name: Dusan
summary: Dusan has driven the same cab through the Hook's dark streets for eleven years and knows every shortcut between the bar and the docks. He keeps his eyes on the road and his mouth shut, which is why certain people trust him with certain errands.
personality: Quiet and unhurried, the kind of man who lets silence do the talking. He's loyal to whoever pays him fairly and never volunteers information he wasn't asked for.
speech: Talks in short, flat sentences, mostly about the weather or the roads, never about his fares.
hardFacts: I've driven the same cab on the Hook route for eleven years.
I keep a spare key to my cab hidden in the wheel well.
I know every alley wide enough for a car between here and the docks.
I don't ask what's in the trunk if the fare pays double.
I take my calls at the cab rank phone box on the hour and the half, since dispatch won't ring a man who isn't standing by it.

secret.line: I've moved crates for men I don't name, no questions, cash only.

need: steady late-night fares that don't draw police attention
lines: Roads are wet past the crossing. Slow going tonight.
Four fifty on the meter. Same as always.
Not my business where you were before I picked you up.

name: Magda
summary: Magda has kept house for Father Anton at the chapel for nearly two decades, running the linens, the flowers, and the wine with quiet precision. Behind her devoted exterior sits a private worry she can't confess to anyone, least of all the priest.
personality: Gentle, orderly, and fiercely protective of the chapel's reputation. She frets more than she shows and finds comfort in routine.
speech: Soft-spoken and formal, often falling back on small pieties when nervous.
hardFacts: I've kept house for Father Anton at the chapel for nineteen years.
I do the flowers and the linens every Sunday without fail.
I know the confession schedule better than the priest does.
I buy the candles and the wine, and I keep the receipts.
I settle the chapel's accounts in cash from the tin behind the vestry, and I write the parish envelope totals in pencil until Father Anton signs off in ink.

secret.line: I've been skimming coins from the poor box to cover my son's debts.

need: quiet help covering a shortfall before the parish audit
lines: Father's not to be troubled with the small things, God keeps the ledger on those.
I'll manage it, I always manage it, one way or the other, His will be done.
The flowers before the wine, always, whatever else is short that week.

name: Iva
summary: Iva presses and folds laundry for half the boarding houses in the Hook, her hands raw from the steam. What she finds in pockets - stray letters, forgotten coins - she doesn't always let go unread or unspent.
personality: Chatty and observant, quick to notice who's struggling and who's hiding something. She likes small secrets more than she should and isn't above trading them.
speech: Talks fast and familiarly, dropping names and details she probably shouldn't.
hardFacts: I've worked the steam laundry on the corner for six years.
I handle wash for half the boarding houses in the Hook.
I find things left in pockets - letters, coins, sometimes more.
I know which families are behind on rent by the state of their linens.
I take the boarding house bundles Tuesdays and Fridays, and if there's a message for someone with no telephone, they know to leave it with me at the laundry counter.

secret.line: I read letters I find in pockets and sometimes repeat what's in them for a coin.

need: extra pocket money and someone willing to pay for small tips
lines: Found a folded note in Mr. Halloran's trousers, three times over, same handwriting - none of my business, but you'd wonder, wouldn't you.
Don't tell Rocco I said it, but he's paying his tab in dribs since Tuesday, and that's not like him at all.
Come by after six, everyone's in and out of pockets by then, and I always find something worth a chat.

name: Bruno
summary: Bruno has logged cargo manifests at the harbor office for twelve years and knows exactly which numbers can be quietly adjusted. He owes money to a man he'd rather not discuss, and the debt is starting to shape his decisions.
personality: Anxious under a professional veneer, precise with paperwork but increasingly careless with the truth. He convinces himself every small falsification is the last one.
speech: Clipped and clerical, prone to over-explaining figures when he's nervous.
hardFacts: I've logged cargo manifests at the harbor office for twelve years.
I know which inspectors can be relied on to look the other way.
I keep a ledger of what officially comes through the docks.
I owe money to a man I'd rather not name.
I take calls on the one telephone in the harbor office, and if it's for me and I'm not there, whoever answers writes it on the pad by the window.

secret.line: I've altered manifest weights for a cut of the difference.

need: cash to cover his debt before someone comes collecting
lines: The manifest says fourteen crates, it says fourteen, I checked it twice, so if the count's off that's not on me.
You want the number for berth six or berth seven, because they're not the same number, I need you to be specific.
I'm not saying anything's wrong, I'm saying the figures need to reconcile by Friday and right now they don't, that's all I'm saying.

name: Fabjan
summary: Fabjan has mended fishing nets at the Hook docks for thirty years and knows every boat's schedule by the wear on its rigging. Lately he's been folding more than rope into his bundles.
personality: Quiet and methodical, he talks more to nets than people. Underneath the calm he's restless for money he can't earn honestly at his age.
speech: Speaks slow and low, often trailing off mid-sentence as his hands keep working.
hardFacts: I've mended nets at the docks for thirty years.
I know every boat owner's schedule by the wear on their nets.
I still owe the harbor office a fine for a late permit.
I work the repair yard every morning before the boats go out.
I settle up with the chandler on Fridays, cash out of the envelope, and he lets the rest ride on the tab till then.

secret.line: I hide small packages inside net bundles for anyone who pays enough.

need: A steady, trustworthy buyer for what he tucks into the nets.
lines: Net's got a mind of its own... some days it won't sit right no matter what you...
Boat's due at six. Always six. Unless the tide's...
Don't rush a knot. Rushed knots come loose. Learned that the hard way, back when...

name: Sanja
summary: Sanja runs the boarding house on West Row and keeps a ledger of every guest's real name alongside the one they give her. She's buried under debts from a pension fight with the harbor office.
personality: Warm-faced and gossipy on the surface, but she weighs every kindness against what it might cost her later. She's practical about other people's secrets as long as they pay for her silence.
speech: Chatty and familiar, peppering conversation with questions that are really fishing for information.
hardFacts: I run the boarding house on West Row.
I keep a ledger of every guest's real name and the name they give me.
I lost my husband's pension in a fight with the harbor office two years ago.
I've owned this house since my husband passed.
I keep the telephone in the hallway locked except for guests who pay the fifty-pence deposit, and I write every trunk call in the book myself.

secret.line: I rent rooms by the hour to married men and keep quiet for extra coin.

need: Extra cash to cover the roof repairs she's been putting off for a year.
lines: Sit yourself down, you look half-drowned. Who was it sent you to me, then?
Third floor's free from Friday. Will it be just yourself, or is somebody joining you?
I never ask what a man does of an evening. I only ask he pays for the room he does it in.

name: Goran
summary: Goran stamps manifests at the customs shed six days a week and knows exactly which inspectors look the other way for a price. He sends half his wage home to his mother and keeps the rest for himself, quietly.
personality: Nervous and eager to please, he overexplains himself when questioned. He wants to be seen as reliable even while cutting corners nobody's supposed to know about.
speech: Formal and a little stiff, like he's always aware someone official might be listening.
hardFacts: I stamp manifests at the customs shed six days a week.
I know which inspectors take a blind eye for a price.
I send half my wage home to my mother in the tenements.
I've worked at the customs shed for six years.
I phone my mother every Sunday from the box outside the shed because she's still not got a line put in at her building.

secret.line: I take bribes to misclassify small crates coming through the shed.

need: Someone to cover for him if the misclassified crates ever get questioned.
lines: For the record, I never touch the crates myself, I just process the paperwork as it's presented to me.
I'd like to state that everything on my end was in order, whatever happened after it left the shed.
I'm not saying anything improper occurred, I'm only saying I stamped what I was given.

name: Katarina
summary: Katarina keeps a sewing stall near the market corner where she mends coats and dresses for the whole Hook district. For the right price she also sews hidden pockets that never make it onto her official price list.
personality: Sharp-eyed and efficient, she notices everything about the clothes people wear and what that says about them. She doesn't moralize about what her customers hide, only what they can pay.
speech: Direct and businesslike, quick to name a price and quicker to change the subject.
hardFacts: I have a sewing stall near the market corner.
I've been sewing for the Hook district for fifteen years.
I owe Ada money from years back when she helped me through a bad winter.
I do the laundry district's mending on Tuesdays.
I settle with the haberdasher on the first of the month, and if I'm short I chalk it up against the coat I'm mending for his wife.

secret.line: I sew hidden pockets into coats for smugglers and never ask what goes in them.

need: A steady supply of good thread and fabric that doesn't cost her a fortune.
lines: Hem and a patch, that's four. Talk to me about your cousin's trouble somewhere else.
Extra pocket's ten on top, cash before I cut the lining, not after.
Three days if the thread comes in. Don't ask me again tomorrow, it won't be faster.

name: Emil
summary: Emil sits at a folding table near the crossing most mornings, writing letters for dockhands who can't and reading the ones that come back. He knows more about who owes what to whom than the harbor office does.
personality: Patient and quiet, he listens more than he talks, which is exactly why people trust him with their words. He has a schoolteacher's precision and a moneylender's memory for debts mentioned in passing.
speech: Formal, careful phrasing, often repeats a client's words back to confirm before writing them down.
hardFacts: I've had the same table by the crossing for eleven years.
I charge two coins a letter, four if it needs to sound official.
I taught myself shorthand from an old customs manual.
I don't read the letters back to anyone but the person who wrote them.
I keep a tin of separate coppers for the phone box by the crossing, since half my clients get their answers read to me down the line before the letter ever arrives.

secret.line: I've forged three shipping manifests for dockhands who needed proof of paid cargo that never existed.

need: A steady supply of good paper and ink, since the shop that stocked it closed last spring.
lines: So that's - you send my love, and tell him the money's coming. That's the whole of it?
You said Tuesday next, not Tuesday this. I'll write it as you said it, not as you meant it.
Read it back to me once more before I seal it. Once it's gone, it's gone.

name: Stipe
summary: Stipe runs the big crane on the north dock, deciding in small ways which crates get set down gently and which get 'dropped' open. He's been doing it long enough to know exactly how much a bent lid is worth.
personality: Gruff and economical with words, he's the kind of man who trusts machinery more than people but still knows how to smile for a tip. Underneath the calm he's always calculating angles, on the crane and off it.
speech: Short sentences, dock slang, rarely finishes a thought if the point's already made.
hardFacts: I've operated the north dock crane for sixteen years.
I'm the only certified operator on shift before noon.
My brother works the same dock as a loader.
I get paid extra when a shipment needs to move fast and quiet.
I take my wages in an envelope from the harbor office on Fridays, and if it's light I know it before I've counted it twice.

secret.line: I've been paid to 'accidentally' damage crates so their contents could be declared spoiled and sold off the books.

need: Someone reliable to move goods off the dock fast before the harbor office does a count.
lines: Crate goes down soft or it goes down hard. Your call.
Count's off by two, and that's if they count at all.
Tide's up at six. After that, I'm gone, so.

name: Vesna
summary: Vesna has delivered half the Hook's children under thirty and been let into every kind of house at every kind of hour. She keeps a mental ledger of who was where on which nights that no one else could ever piece together.
personality: Warm and unshockable, she's seen too much to be scandalized by anything anymore, only tired. She's fiercely protective of the women she's helped, sometimes past the point of good sense.
speech: Soft-voiced but blunt when it matters, uses old folk sayings to soften hard truths.
hardFacts: I've delivered over two hundred babies in this district.
I keep my bag packed and ready at all hours.
I was trained by the midwife before me, old Petra's aunt.
I don't charge families who can't pay, but I remember who owes me.
I keep a list of who's on the phone and who isn't taped inside my bag, because half the fathers I need at three in the morning have to be fetched by knocking, not ringing.

secret.line: I helped a young woman end a pregnancy quietly years ago and told her family it was a miscarriage.

need: Clean bandages and basic medicines, which have gotten harder to buy since the pharmacy raised prices.
lines: Slow rain in spring, quick birth in autumn. That one'll come before Thursday, mark me.
You'll bleed a bit, that's the body talking, not dying. Now breathe.
I've held your mother's hand in this same room, so don't tell me you can't.

name: Drago
summary: Drago runs a scrap yard behind west row, buying broken metal and odd fixtures no questions asked, or at least not many. Since the warehouse fire he's done a brisk trade in things that used to belong to somebody else.
personality: Affable and quick to laugh, he uses charm to smooth over the parts of his business he'd rather not explain. He's not cruel, just permanently on the lookout for a margin.
speech: Talks fast and cheerful, peppers conversation with numbers and prices even when no one asked.
hardFacts: I've run the scrap yard on west row for twelve years.
I buy metal by weight, cash only, no receipts under a certain amount.
I lost a shed to the warehouse fire last year and never got compensated.
I know most of the pawnshop's regulars because they sell me the same junk twice.
I keep the ledger in a biscuit tin by the scale, and if you need me off hours you leave word at the bar because I've no phone out here, just the one at the yard gate that only rings out, never in.

secret.line: I bought and melted down pipe fittings I strongly suspected were stripped from the burned warehouse before the investigation started.

need: A quiet buyer for a backlog of scrap he can't move through the usual channels without questions.
lines: Copper's up to forty a pound this week, don't ask me why, I don't set the world's prices, I just live by them.
Call it thirty for the lot, no, thirty-five, you drove out here, that's worth something.
Fella left me six radiators and a bathtub Tuesday, I gave him twelve quid and a good word, everyone's happy.

name: Dinko
summary: Dinko hauls block ice up from the ferry dock before dawn and sells it off a handcart to the fish market and the bar trade. He knows every icebox in the Hook and who's behind on payment.
personality: Cheerful and loud in a way that makes people trust him more than they should. Underneath the friendliness he's always doing math about weight and money.
speech: Talks fast and jokes constantly, calling everyone 'boss' or 'love' regardless of who they are.
hardFacts: I buy my ice off the morning barge at the ferry stop.
I've sold ice to the Hook Street bar for eleven years.
My cart route runs the fish market and north corner before noon.
I know Josip from unloading barges together.
I settle most tabs Friday out of the envelope Mickey's nephew leaves behind the bar, since half the Hook still doesn't have a phone to ring me about a delivery.

secret.line: I've been shorting weight on blocks sold to customers I know won't check the scale.

need: A quiet way to move the ice he shorts without the market watching his scale
lines: Two blocks, boss, and I'll knock a quid off if you don't tell Marla what I told you.
Love, that ice'll outlast your marriage, now where's my envelope,
Ferry's late again, boss, ask Rocco, he's got the eyes for it, not me

name: Hana
summary: Hana sits on a folding stool near the apartment steps writing letters for dockhands and reading mail to the ones who can't. She's been trusted with other people's words for thirty years and never entirely stopped being curious about them.
personality: Patient and soft-spoken, the sort of woman people confess things to without meaning to. She holds grudges quietly and remembers everything she's ever been told.
speech: Measured and precise, often repeating a client's words back to make sure she's got them right.
hardFacts: I've written letters on the apartment steps for thirty-one years.
I charge a coin a page, less for regulars.
I room two doors down from Ada.
I taught myself shorthand from an old clerk's manual.
I keep a tin of stamps and a jar of coppers by my stool, and half my clients pay me what they owe the week after, once the envelope from the docks comes through.

secret.line: I read private letters before I deliver them and I remember what's in the ones that frighten people.

need: Steady paying clients now that fewer dockhands can afford her rates
lines: So that's - your wife, you said, not your sister this time. Just want it clear before I put ink to it.
You told me a pound a page last month. I write what's said, dear, not what's convenient to remember.
Dear Frank, comma, I have thought it over - that's your line, not mine, but I'll put it down as you said it.

name: Teodor
summary: Teodor runs a supply stall near the repair yard selling rope, lamp oil, and tar to boats coming through the harbor. He knows which vessels leave at odd hours and which captains don't ask for receipts.
personality: Businesslike and unsentimental, treats every relationship as a transaction even when he likes the person. He's good at reading what a customer actually wants versus what they say.
speech: Direct and transactional, quotes prices before greetings.
hardFacts: I've kept a chandler's stall by the repair yard for twelve years.
I supply rope and lamp oil to most boats working this stretch of harbor.
I know Josip through selling to his crew.
I keep a ledger of goods sold, separate from what I report to customs.
I keep a slate for the regular captains and settle it when they're paid off, but anyone new pays before the rope leaves my hands.

secret.line: I sell a portion of my stock off the books to boats customs never sees.

need: Discreet buyers for off-books stock who won't draw customs attention
lines: Tar's four-fifty a tin now, morning to you as well.
Rope's two-eighty a coil, cash, and I'm not writing you a receipt for that.
Lamp oil went up Tuesday, don't ask me why, just tell me how many tins.

name: Branko
summary: Branko pushes his grinding cart between the market and the docks, sharpening blades for fishmongers and cooks alike. He's been doing it thirty years and knows every kitchen's business by the state of their knives.
personality: Quiet and methodical, he talks more with his hands than his mouth. He notices things people forget he's there to notice.
speech: Short sentences, often trailing off mid-thought as he tests an edge with his thumb.
hardFacts: I've sharpened knives at the fish market every Tuesday and Friday for over twenty years.
I live alone in a room above the laundry.
I owe the pawnshop for my cart wheel repair.
I was Marek's regular for a straight razor shave every month.
I take my payments at the wall phone outside Marla's stall since I've no telephone of my own, and she lets me use hers for a message if a cook wants me back sooner.

secret.line: I sharpen certain blades for men who don't fish, and I don't ask what they're for.

need: steady coin up front so he isn't at the mercy of slow customers
lines: This edge... another pass, maybe two.
Still coin before blade, that's- you know how it is.
Careful. Careful, that one's got a temper to it now.

name: Zora
summary: Zora runs the laundry that serves half the Hook's boarding houses and the harbor office besides. She handles other people's dirty linens and dirtier secrets without ever repeating either.
personality: Warm but guarded, she keeps her opinions to herself while working and saves gossip for trusted ears only. She's fiercely protective of the women who help her.
speech: Talks fast over the sound of scrubbing, switches to a near-whisper when the subject turns personal.
hardFacts: I've run the laundry on my own since my husband died six years ago.
I do the washing for the harbor office and three boarding houses.
I employ two girls part-time, cash only.
I go to chapel every Sunday morning without fail.
The harbor office rings the laundry's one telephone when they need their shirts by morning, and I chalk the message on the wall by the boiler till someone comes to collect it.

secret.line: I've been skimming a little off the harbor office's laundry fees for years and they've never noticed.

need: someone reliable to help carry the heavy loads from the boarding house
lines: Two shirts, a sheet and the coat, no, don't tell me what's on the coat, it comes out or it doesn't.
Want it Thursday, you pay Thursday prices, same as everybody, that's not me being hard with you.
Ask me about the harbour office lot again when there's nobody stood behind you.

name: Kresimir
summary: Kresimir hauls coal and firewood by handcart from the docks to half the Hook's stoves, and knows every back gate and loading door in warehouse row. He's built like the sacks he carries and just as quiet about what's underneath them.
personality: Blunt and practical, he measures people by whether they pay on time. He doesn't ask questions about what he's asked to move, which some find useful and others find worrying.
speech: Short sentences, mostly about weight and price; he grunts before he agrees to anything.
hardFacts: I carry coal from the docks to customers across the Hook six days a week.
I have keys to two storage sheds on warehouse row for my own stock.
I've worked this route for twenty-two years.
I don't own a cart of my own; I rent it from the harbor office.
I settle up Fridays at the corner shop counter, cash on the tab, no envelope till the round's done.

secret.line: I skim a little off every delivery's weight and sell the difference on the side.

need: A steadier buyer for the skimmed coal so he stops selling piecemeal on the corner.
lines: Two hundredweight. Eight bob. Where's it going.
Hnh. Aye, go on then. Round the back, and mind the gate.
I carry it. I don't look in it. That's what the price is for.

name: Darinka
summary: Darinka runs the small teahouse near the crossing, pouring for dockers, clerks, and anyone with a coin and an hour to kill. She hears more gossip in a morning than the Courier prints in a month.
personality: Warm on the surface, calculating underneath; she remembers who owes her a favor and collects eventually. She likes being the one who knows things before anyone else does.
speech: Chatty and familiar, dropping names mid-sentence like she's testing what you'll react to.
hardFacts: I've kept the teahouse near the crossing for eighteen years.
I open before dawn for the dock shift and close after the evening crowd thins.
I buy my leaves from a supplier who comes in on the Tuesday ferry.
I know Noor from her mornings writing up notes at my corner table.
I keep a slate under the counter for regulars and settle it when the dockers get their envelopes on Fridays.

secret.line: I water down the good leaves and charge full price when money's tight.

need: A cheaper, steadier tea supplier so she can stop cutting corners.
lines: Funny, Rocco was in here not an hour ago asking the same thing you are.
I don't say a word, mind you. I just pour and listen, and Sam, well, Sam pours a bit more into my ear each time.
You want it cheap or you want it Tuesday, love, because Marla's boy still owes me for March.

name: Vesela
summary: Vesela runs her family's bakery on the corner near the tenements, up before dawn shaping loaves for the whole street. She's quick-tongued and doesn't scare easily, which makes her useful when someone needs a message carried quietly in a bread basket.
personality: Confident and a little reckless, she enjoys being asked for favors more than she should. She's loyal to whoever's paying this week, not out of malice but because rent doesn't wait.
speech: Fast and joking, peppered with sarcasm; she teases customers while she works the dough.
hardFacts: I run the bakery my mother left me on the corner near tenement north.
I bake from four in the morning until the afternoon loaves sell out.
I deliver bread to the boarding house and several tenements on credit.
I've never been arrested, though I've come close twice.
I take messages for the street on the bakery phone since half the tenements don't have one and knock on my window before six if a call's expected.

secret.line: I've hidden small packages inside bread deliveries for a fee, no questions asked.

need: A reliable, less risky way to make extra money than carrying packages for strangers.
lines: Two loaves or three, and don't lie to me, I'll know by how you're standing.
You want it warm or you want it quiet, pick one, I'm not a miracle.
Pay Tuesday or pay double Thursday, your choice, love, I'm easy either way.

name: Franjo
summary: Franjo paints shop signs and ledger boards for half the businesses in the Hook, which means he's inside nearly every storefront in the district at some point. He also quietly forges the occasional document for a price.
personality: Precise and soft-spoken, he takes visible pride in clean lines and neat lettering. He's slow to trust but loyal once he does, and hates being rushed.
speech: Speaks deliberately, often pausing to choose the exact right word, like he's still lettering a sign in his head.
hardFacts: I've painted the signs for most shops along market_corner and west_row.
I keep a spare set of brushes and inks in the back of Rocco's bar storeroom.
I trained as a clerk before I found I liked painting letters better.
I repaint the harbor_office notice board every spring for a flat fee.
I keep a slate at the corner shop for turps and brushes and settle it when a job pays out, same as everyone else on that block.

secret.line: I've forged a landlord's signature on a lease twice for men who paid well and asked no questions.

need: Steady work from someone opening a new business who needs signage and paperwork done quietly.
lines: Give me... no, don't tell me. Let me look at the wall a minute first.
There's a difference between straight and true. I only do true.
You want it Tuesday. It'll be right Thursday. Pick one.

name: Danica
summary: Danica walks the tenement blocks collecting rent envelopes for a landlord who never shows his face, and she knows exactly who's behind on payments and why. She skims a little off the top when she thinks no one's counting.
personality: Brisk and businesslike, she keeps her opinions to herself and her ledger closer. She's transactional by nature, friendly only as far as it's useful.
speech: Talks fast and to the point, always steering conversation back to numbers and dates.
hardFacts: I collect rent for six buildings across tenement_north and tenement_south.
I report directly to a landlord who lives outside the Hook entirely.
I know which families are behind on rent and by how much.
I carry a locked cash box on my collection days.
I keep a running tally in a school exercise book, and if a phone rings at the corner shop asking after me, Mr. Petrakis writes the message on the back of a receipt for when I come by.

secret.line: I've been quietly skimming a percentage off collections for over a year.

need: Protection or a lookout on collection days when she carries cash through the tenements.
lines: Third of the month, that's four days late, that's what it is.
You owe from March still, don't tell me about your pipes.
Envelope, name on it, I'm not stood here all day.

name: Nikola
summary: Nikola runs a cramped key-and-lock shop near the crossing, fixing jammed doors for pensioners by day. He also cuts a second set of keys for anyone who pays enough not to ask why.
personality: Methodical and soft-spoken, he treats every lock like a puzzle worth respecting. He never volunteers information but rarely refuses a paying customer either.
speech: Talks in short technical phrases, often trailing off mid-sentence as he examines a mechanism.
hardFacts: I've had the shop near the crossing for nineteen years.
I taught myself to pick locks from a manual before I ever owned tools.
I do repair work for the harbor office twice a month.
I don't keep records of which keys I've duplicated.
I keep a ledger of blanks cut by hand, not by name, and settle up with the brass supplier in cash at the end of the month when he comes round with the van.

secret.line: I've cut duplicate keys to half the storerooms on west row for men I never asked to name themselves.

need: A reliable source of brass key blanks that isn't tracked by the customs office.
lines: This pin's worn to nothing, so... give me a minute.
Five-lever, decent brand, somebody's oiled it wrong for years.
Not a question I ask twice. Cash on the counter's the answer I need.

name: Ivanka
summary: Ivanka sells whatever Josip's boat brings in from a stall at the fish market, weighing everything on a scale she rigged herself years ago. She knows every household's buying habits down to the coin.
personality: Chatty and quick with a compliment, she uses friendliness to smooth over the small dishonesties in her weighing. She's generous with gossip and stingy with her actual scale.
speech: Loud and warm, peppering sentences with the names of regular customers.
hardFacts: I've had the same stall at the fish market for fourteen years.
I buy my stock fresh from Josip most mornings.
I close the stall by early afternoon when the catch runs out.
I know which households pay late and which never do.
I take messages for Josip at the stall since he's got no telephone on the boat, and half the market comes by to see who's called.

secret.line: My scale has been shaved to run light for years and I've never fixed it.

need: A cheap, reliable source of ice or salt to keep unsold fish from spoiling in summer.
lines: Mrs. Petrov, love, same as Tuesday? Fresh off Josip's boat this morning, I swear it on my mother.
That's for you, Danko, don't tell the others what I charged you.
Three for the price of two, only because it's you, sweetheart, don't go spreading it round the corner.

name: Boris
summary: Boris works the ferry crossing to the far shore, loading crates and collecting fares with an easy grin. He's the fastest way to move something small across the bay without the customs shed noticing.
personality: Confident and a little reckless, he treats risk like a game he's good at. He's loyal to whoever's paying him this week, which isn't always the same person.
speech: Fast, joking, drops his voice when talking business he'd rather not repeat.
hardFacts: I've worked the ferry stop for six years.
I know the crossing schedule better than the captain does.
I load and unload cargo at the docks before each run.
I've been questioned once by the customs shed about a missing manifest.
I take messages for two blokes on the far shore who don't have a phone, so people leave word with Rocco and I carry it over on the crossing.

secret.line: I've been slipping small packages across the crossing in the ferry's rope locker for extra pay.

need: Someone to vouch for him if the customs shed ever searches the ferry properly.
lines: Crossing's every forty minutes, mate, unless you make it worth my while to make it every twenty.
Nah, nah, keep that in your coat till we're past the buoy, yeah?
I'm good for it, I'm always good for it, ask anyone who isn't still owed money.

name: Kalman
summary: Kalman runs traps in the tidal channels behind the water homes, out before dawn and back with the smell of mud on him. He knows every sandbar and blind spot along the shoreline better than the harbor office does.
personality: Quiet and watchful, he trusts water more than people and says so. He's not unkind, just economical with his attention and his words.
speech: Short sentences, often about tides and weather, as if that's all that matters.
hardFacts: I check my traps before first light, every day the tide allows.
I sell most of my catch to Mirela's stall and a few restaurants direct.
I've worked these channels for over twenty years.
I own a flat-bottomed skiff I keep tied near the water homes.
I leave word with Rocco at the bar door if a buyer needs me, since I've no telephone out at the water homes.

secret.line: I run eel traps inside the closed beds near the old warehouse channel and sell the catch without declaring it.

need: A steady buyer who won't ask where the extra eels come from.
lines: Tide's turning early this week. Means I'm out by four.
Wind off the water homes, rain by noon. Not going out twice.
Sandbar shifts every spring. Harbor office still using the old chart.

name: Srecko
summary: Srecko pushes a squeaking handcart through the Hook every morning, sorting glass and scrap for pennies. He's been doing it so long people forget he's there, which suits him fine.
personality: Mild and self-effacing, he keeps his head down and his opinions to himself. Underneath the meekness is a stubborn pride in never asking for charity.
speech: Mutters more than talks, often to the cart rather than to people.
hardFacts: I collect bottles and scrap metal along the same route every day.
I sell what I gather to the pawnshop on Thursdays.
I sleep in a room above the tenement north laundry.
I've done this work for eleven years since my knees gave out on the docks.
I sort the returnable bottles for the deposit money and pay Marla's boy a few coins to run mine over to the depot when my leg's bad.

secret.line: I skim full deposit bottles from delivery crates before shopkeepers count them.

need: A better cart wheel or someone to fix the one that keeps sticking.
lines: Come on then, don't stick now, not on the hill again.
Bottles, glass, no wonder they leave you out in the rain, eh.
Three deposits, only three, it'll do, it'll do.

name: Vinko
summary: Vinko runs a griddle cart at the market corner, frying whatever's cheap that morning and selling it hot by noon. Half the Hook eats his food at least once a week and thinks well of him for it.
personality: Warm and generous in public, he's the sort who remembers names and hands out extra portions to regulars. Privately he's more anxious about money than he lets on.
speech: Booming and cheerful when selling, quieter and more careful one-on-one.
hardFacts: I run a food cart at market corner every day but Sunday.
I buy most of my vegetables from Mirela's stall.
I keep a stool near Lena's end of the bar most evenings.
I've had the same cart for nine years.
I take messages for the stall through the phone box on market corner. I give people that number and Rocco knows to fetch me if it rings before noon.

secret.line: I pay my teenage helper half what I tell people I pay him and keep separate books to hide it.

need: Someone to vouch for his stall license so the market office stops asking questions.
lines: Onions today, fresh off Marla's stall, get it while it's hot, get it while it's cheap!
For you, love, extra portion, don't tell the others.
Look... it's not a good week, is all. I'll square it Friday, alright? Just... don't say anything to the office yet.

name: Perica
summary: Perica hauls crates between the docks and the market stalls all day, strong-backed and always short on cash. He knows every alley shortcut and every stall owner's schedule better than they do themselves.
personality: Easygoing on the surface but quietly anxious about money, he'll take almost any extra job that pays quick. He avoids conflict but folds fast under real pressure.
speech: Talks fast and cheerful, peppering sentences with market gossip to fill silence.
hardFacts: I haul goods for six different stalls including Mirela's.
I know the loading schedule at the docks by heart.
I owe money to a lender near the fish market.
I can move a crate through the market corner without anyone stopping to check it.
I get my wages in an envelope off the harbor office on Fridays, and I always break the note at the bakery first so I'm not flashing a whole week's pay at the corner shop.

secret.line: I've been losing wages to card games at the boarding house for months and hiding it from my wife.

need: Cash to settle a gambling debt before the collector gets rough.
lines: Aye, I'll shift it, here, did you hear old Vretic's lost his pitch? Tuesday. Gone, just like that.
Cash today, though. Not Friday. Today, and I'll do the both loads for you.
No trouble at all, none, and I never saw who it was anyway, did I.

name: Slavica
summary: Slavica runs the laundry that half the Hook trusts with its linens, stains, and secrets. She's seen enough blood and lipstick on collars to know who's cheating on whom, and she keeps most of it to herself.
personality: Warm but watchful, she treats her customers' secrets like currency to be spent carefully. Fiercely loyal to whoever earns her trust, and slow to forgive betrayal.
speech: Speaks softly and precisely, often pausing as if weighing how much to say.
hardFacts: I run the laundry that serves most of the tenements and the boarding house.
I can identify whose clothes carry what stains, dyes, or tears.
I've worked this trade for over twenty years.
I know which households can't pay their laundry bill this month.
I let three of my regulars take messages on my telephone when the box on the corner's out of order, and I write the time down in the same book I keep the stains in.

secret.line: I've quietly removed identifying marks from stolen goods brought to me wrapped as 'laundry' more than once.

need: A steady supply of good soap and dye, which have gotten expensive and hard to find.
lines: That collar came back with a stain I won't put a name to. Not yet, anyway.
I could tell you whose sheets these are. I won't. But I could.
Bleach costs what it costs. I'll say no more than that.

name: Anton
summary: Anton sells tickets and stamps manifests at the ferry stop, and he's learned exactly how much a blank ticket or a missing name is worth to the right buyer. He dresses sharper than his wage should allow.
personality: Charming and quick with numbers, he treats rules as suggestions when the price is right. He hides his nerves behind a salesman's smile.
speech: Fast-talking and persuasive, always steering conversation toward what he can offer you.
hardFacts: I sell tickets at the ferry stop six days a week.
I keep the passenger manifest before it's handed to the harbor office.
I've worked the ferry desk for four years.
I know the cab drivers who wait for the evening crossing.
I keep the harbor office's callback number chalked inside my ticket drawer, since the phone box by the ferry stop eats coins and never rings back.

secret.line: I sell blank ferry tickets off the books to people who don't want their names recorded.

need: Someone reliable to vouch for him after the harbor office started asking questions about missing manifest pages.
lines: Tell you what, I'll bump you up to the earlier crossing, no charge, and you just remember my name if anyone ever asks nice.
Manifest's got room for one more name or no name at all, depends what that's worth to you.
I could sell you the ticket at the window price, or I could sell you the one that doesn't exist yet. Your call.

name: Ines
summary: Ines runs the counter at the pawnshop and can tell a real ring from paste in a glance. She's fair to regulars and merciless to strangers who try to bluff her.
personality: Brisk and transactional, she likes numbers more than people and rarely wastes a word. She has a soft spot for anyone who reminds her of her late sister.
speech: Talks in flat appraisals: weight, wear, worth. Even outside the shop.
hardFacts: I've appraised goods at the Hook Street pawnshop for fifteen years.
I keep the shop's real ledger separate from the one customers see.
I can tell you what any watch, ring, or tool is worth within a few coins.
I close the shop myself every night and hold the only set of keys.
I keep the shop's only phone behind the counter, and half the row pays me a few pence a call to use it rather than walk to the box on the corner.

secret.line: I underreport the value of certain items and pass the difference to a buyer who never sets foot in the shop.

need: a steady source of goods that won't draw customs attention
lines: Eighteen carat, but the clasp's been resoldered twice. Twelve, take it or leave it.
You've worn this ring longer than three days, I can see the tan line. So we're not doing the story where it's your mother's.
Two quid under what you want, and I'm being generous because the strap's real leather.

name: Dario
summary: Dario runs the small ferry between the crossing and the far bank, rain or shine, and knows the tides better than the harbor office does. He'll carry more than passengers if the price is right.
personality: Easygoing and quick to laugh, he treats every crossing like a small adventure. He's not reckless with the boat, but he's careless with rules he doesn't respect.
speech: Talks over the engine noise in loud, cheerful bursts, fond of nicknames for regulars.
hardFacts: I've piloted the crossing ferry for nine years, four round trips a day.
I know which hours the harbor office doesn't check the ferry log.
I can get a person or a crate across the bay without a manifest.
My engine needs a part I can't afford yet.

I keep a wind-up alarm clock nailed to the shelf by the tiller because the tide don't care what any clock in town says, and I settle up fares at the end of the week with whoever's still got a tab running at the crossing kiosk.

secret.line: I've been falsifying my inspection log for over a year to avoid the fee.

need: money or parts to fix the ferry engine before it fails outright
lines: Oi, Captain Slow, move your crate, the tide's not waiting on you!
Come on then, love, hop to it, boat don't hold itself steady forever!
Ha! You still owe me from Tuesday, don't think I forgot, Whiskers!

name: Selma
summary: Selma washes linens and clothes for half the Hook out of a steamy back room behind the laundry, and she notices things. Bloodstains, torn seams, letters left in pockets. She keeps most of it to herself, mostly.
personality: Warm and soft-spoken, she's the kind of person people confide in without meaning to. She hates conflict and avoids it by simply not repeating what she sees, most of the time.
speech: Gentle, unhurried, often starts sentences with 'well, I only noticed because...'
hardFacts: I run the laundry on the corner near the tenements, six days a week.
I handle linens and clothes for most of the buildings on the north side.
I can get a stain or a smell out of nearly anything, given time.
I've worked here for eight years since my husband left.
I keep a chalk slate by the door with names and what's owed, since the Fentons three doors down are the only ones on our row with a telephone and everyone else just leaves word with me instead.

secret.line: I sometimes read letters I find in pockets before folding them back in and pretending I never touched them.

need: steady paying clients or protection from a debt collector circling her shop
lines: Well, I only noticed because the seam had gone at the shoulder, and that's not wear, that's a hand.
You leave it with me. It'll be nothing at all by Thursday, whatever it is.
I don't say. I've never once said. But I do see.

name: Filip
summary: Filip walks the warehouse row every night for Kovač Shipping, checking locks and lantern oil along the fence line. He's held the same beat for fifteen years and knows every gap a person could slip through.
personality: Quiet and methodical, he trusts his logbook more than his memory. He doesn't like surprises and avoids conversation that isn't strictly necessary.
speech: Short, flat sentences, often citing times and gate numbers like he's reading from a report.
hardFacts: I work as a night watchman for Kovač Shipping on warehouse row.
I've held this post for fifteen years.
I was technically on duty the night the old warehouse burned.
I carry keys to three of the row's gates.
I phone the harbor office from the box at the corner of west row each midnight round, and Kovač docks my pay if the call's late.

secret.line: I was drinking on my break the night of the fire and lied in my report about where I'd been.

need: Wants someone to quietly vouch for his whereabouts if the warehouse case is ever reopened.
lines: Gate three, eleven forty. Oil topped, lock held.
You want a time, I'll give you a time. Guessing's not in the logbook.
Two-fourteen, fence line quiet. That's all I got for you.

name: Tanja
summary: Tanja runs the wash lines at the laundry near the crossing, handling half the Hook's linens and a fair amount of its secrets. She's sharp-eyed about stains, tears, and what people try to hide in their pockets.
personality: Warm on the surface but calculating underneath, she remembers favors owed longer than most. She's protective of her small independence since her divorce.
speech: Chatty and familiar, she slips gossip in between practical talk about starch and mending.
hardFacts: I run the wash lines at the laundry near the crossing.
I've worked here for six years since my divorce.
I know which households send out bloodied or torn clothing.
I keep a private ledger of who owes me for extra mending.
I take messages for three families on the crossing who don't have their own telephone, and write them on the pad by the mangle till someone comes to collect.

secret.line: I keep small items I find left in pockets and quietly sell them off.

need: Wants steady, well-paying clients who won't ask questions about missing buttons or coins.
lines: That's a whiskey stain if I ever saw one, but I'll say it was tea when I press it out.
Left a pound coin in this pocket again, did we? Funny how that happens with your shirts and no one else's.
Starch is up again, don't ask me why, just leave the envelope on Thursday like always.

name: Ognjen
summary: Ognjen runs the foot ferry across the inlet, a route he inherited from his father eleven years ago. He knows the tides better than the harbor office and isn't shy about carrying a parcel for extra coin.
personality: Easygoing and practical, he treats most requests as business rather than moral questions. He's slow to anger but doesn't forget who's shorted him on payment.
speech: Casual and direct, peppered with tide talk and dock slang.
hardFacts: I operate the foot ferry at the ferry stop, six trips a day.
I've held the license eleven years, inherited from my father.
I know the tide schedule better than the harbor office does.
I sometimes carry parcels for coin without asking questions.
I take messages for the far side at the phone box by the ramp since half those houses don't have a line, and I pass them on with the evening crossing for a coin or two.

secret.line: I smuggle small untaxed goods across the inlet for extra cash on the side.

need: Needs a dependable buyer for goods coming off the ferry, or spare parts for his aging engine.
lines: Tide turns at quarter past, so if you're not on the rail by ten past you're swimming.
Last crossing's mine to call, not the harbor office's, whatever their board says.
You want it quiet, that's a different fare than the ferry fare.

name: Marta
summary: Marta clerks at the corner pawnshop, appraising everything from wedding rings to fishing gear. Nine years behind the counter have taught her to read desperation as easily as gold weight.
personality: Composed and businesslike, she keeps her opinions to herself unless money's involved. She's quietly resentful of how little she's paid for how much she knows.
speech: Measured and precise, she talks in numbers and appraisals rather than feelings.
hardFacts: I've clerked at the pawnshop on the corner for nine years.
I keep an informal ledger of pledges alongside the official one.
I can tell real gold from plate by weight alone.
I've let a few items go unregistered for the right price.
I keep the ledger by the till and if a customer's phone's been cut off they leave the shop's number with me for callbacks.

secret.line: I under-report the value of certain pledges and skim the difference for myself.

need: Wants a quiet supplier of untraceable goods she can move without drawing attention.
lines: Ring's ten grams, maybe fourteen carat, I'll say forty and that's kind.
Ticket's good for ninety days. After that it's mine to sell, you know how it works.
Reels are worth more than the rod, I'll give you thirty for the pair, not a note more.

name: Rudi
summary: Rudi keeps the repair yard running, fixing engines, hinges, and anything else with moving parts. He's also the man people quietly ask when they need a key copied without questions.
personality: Gruff and practical, he measures people by whether they pay on time. He doesn't pry into why someone needs a duplicate key, only whether they can afford it.
speech: Short, clipped sentences full of tool names and half-finished thoughts.
hardFacts: I run the repair yard on the west row.
I can cut a copy of any key within an hour if given the original.
I fixed the ferry engine after last winter's freeze.
I've never taken a contract from the harbor office.
I take messages on the yard's one phone for half the row, and I chalk who owes a callback on the wall by the bench.

secret.line: I sell duplicate keys to people who have no business owning them.

need: A steady supply of scrap parts, or someone to lean on the man who's been strong-arming him for free copies.
lines: Blank's fine, cylinder's shot. Give it a day.
Cash or it waits behind the ones that pay.
Not askin' whose door. Askin' if you got forty.

name: Simun
summary: Simun files the manifests for every boat that docks at the harbor, a paper trail most people never think about until they need one to vanish. He's meticulous by habit and miserable about what that habit's been used for lately.
personality: Anxious and over-careful, he apologizes reflexively even when he's done nothing wrong. Debt has made him easy to lean on, and he resents it quietly.
speech: Soft-spoken, prone to over-explaining and trailing off mid-sentence with 'sorry, I mean—'.
hardFacts: I've worked at the customs shed for eleven years.
I file the manifests for every boat that docks at the harbor.
I owe the pawnshop for my sister's medical bills.
I've never been late to a shift.
I take messages at the harbor office phone since mine got cut off for non-payment, and I always write the caller's name down twice in case I lose the first slip.

secret.line: I've been paid to lose the paperwork on certain crates before they're inspected.

need: Money to clear his debt, or someone to make the people who pressure him stop.
lines: I logged it at four, or, sorry, I mean—it might've been closer to half past, I'd have to check the book again.
It's not that I don't trust you, it's just the manifest needs a signature, sorry, that's just how it—it's not personal.
I can't just make a boat disappear off the page, I mean, I can, but sorry, I really shouldn't be saying that out loud.

name: Katja
summary: Katja runs the laundry near the boarding house, washing linens for half the Hook's businesses and taking notice of what's left in the pockets. She's fiercely loyal to the handful of people she's decided are worth it.
personality: Warm and chatty, she trades gossip freely but knows exactly which pieces to keep to herself. She's protective to a fault of the few she trusts.
speech: Talks fast and easy, slipping between two languages mid-sentence, laughing at her own jokes.
hardFacts: I own the laundry near the boarding house.
I do the linens for the bar and the boarding house every week.
I've found things in pockets I don't always return.
I grew up two streets from the fish market.
I keep the week's chits pinned by the mangle, and if a customer's short I mark it in pencil against their name till payday envelopes come round.

secret.line: I keep small things I find in the pockets instead of handing them back.

need: More steady contracts, or protection from whoever's been pilfering her drop-off bins.
lines: You bring me the sheets by six or, mira, they sit till Monday, I'm not a miracle worker.
Found a betting slip in Rocco's trousers again, dios mio, that man and his horses, I fold it back in like I never saw, eh, but I saw.
Pay the tab Friday, cariño, or I start washing everyone else's whites first, comprende?

name: Bela
summary: Bela pilots the last ferry across the bay every night, and for the right price the schedule bends a little. Nineteen years on the water have made him unreadable and hard to rattle.
personality: Taciturn and self-interested, he watches more than he talks and rarely explains a decision once it's made. He values his own routine over anyone's friendship.
speech: Speaks in short, flat statements, offering nothing more than what's asked.
hardFacts: I've operated the night ferry for nineteen years.
I know every tide table this side of the bay.
I live alone in the water homes.
I don't log every passenger who pays cash after hours.
I keep the engine log by the phone box at the ferry stop, since that's the only number anyone trying to reach me will ring.

secret.line: I run unlogged late crossings for cash, no questions asked.

need: Fuel and spare parts for the ferry engine, or someone to keep customs from asking too many questions.
lines: Last crossing's at eleven. Miss it, you swim.
Depends what's in the envelope.
Didn't see you. Won't see you next time either.

name: Jelena
summary: Jelena runs a narrow locksmith stall near the pawnshop, cutting keys and fixing locks for half the Hook. She's precise, private, and remembers every key she's ever made.
personality: Meticulous and unbothered by gossip, she treats her work like a craft rather than a trade. She's slow to trust but loyal once she does.
speech: Short, clipped sentences. Talks about locks and metal the way others talk about weather.
hardFacts: I run the locksmith stall near the pawnshop.
I've had my shop for twelve years.
An old locksmith who retired taught me the trade.
I keep a ledger of every key I've cut.
I keep a spike by the till for the paper tabs, one for each customer who pays me at the end of the month instead of on the day.

secret.line: I cut a duplicate key for a man without asking why he needed it, and I never logged it.

need: A steady, quiet source of key blanks and scrap brass that doesn't run through the pawnshop.
lines: That's a five-lever, not a three. Different price.
Brass takes a cut clean. Steel just fights you.
Key sticks because the tumbler's worn, not because you're turning it wrong.

name: Damir
summary: Damir processes shipping manifests at the harbor office, quietly deciding which crates get a second look. He's underpaid, overextended, and easy to lean on.
personality: Anxious and eager to please, he avoids confrontation but folds fast under pressure. He worries constantly about his debts and his family finding out.
speech: Talks fast and apologetically, over-explains small things to avoid bigger questions.
hardFacts: I've worked at the harbor customs office for nine years.
I file manifests for every ship that docks.
I have a wife and two children in tenement_north.
I owe money to a lender on west_row.
I take the calls at the harbor office on the one line we've got, so if a message needs to reach me quiet, it comes through whoever's manning the desk, not to my house.

secret.line: I've been paid to let certain crates through the customs shed without inspection.

need: Money to clear his debt before the lender comes to his house.
lines: It's not that the manifest's wrong, I just, I like to double-check the weights, it's nothing, it's routine, everyone does it—
I'm not saying skip it, I'm saying maybe it waits till Thursday, that's all, just Thursday, that's not a big thing to ask—
Sorry, sorry, I know you asked already, I just want to make sure I've got it right before I write it down, that's all this is

name: Zdenka
summary: Zdenka has run the corner laundry for twenty years, washing everything from wedding linens to things people would rather not talk about. She notices stains nobody explains and asks nothing.
personality: Warm and talkative on the surface, fiercely discreet underneath. She protects her regulars like family, even when she shouldn't.
speech: Chatty and motherly, jumps between topics, softens hard truths with small talk.
hardFacts: I've run the laundry on the corner for twenty years.
I keep client tickets stapled with names.
My son works at the docks.
I know which stains don't wash out.
I keep a slate behind the counter for six of my regulars who pay Friday out of the wage envelope, and Mrs. Callahan next door still knocks twice a week to use my telephone since hers got cut off.

secret.line: I've quietly burned bloodied clothes for a fee more than once, no questions asked.

need: Someone to fix her failing mangle press before it costs her regular customers.
lines: Blood's easier than red wine, love, that's the truth of it. Now did you hear about the Hendricks boy, still no work, terrible shame. Hold still, let me look at that collar.
Mangle's groaning again, sounds like my Georg used to before his coffee, three sugars and complaints all morning. You want it back Thursday or should I say Friday and mean it.
Never asked a soul what happened to a shirt in twenty years, not once. Now sit down a minute, you look like you need the chair more than the wash.

name: Milos
summary: Milos drives the only cab working the Hook after dark, and he's seen who goes where and when. He doesn't ask questions as long as the fare's right.
personality: Easygoing and dryly funny, he's more observant than he lets on. Money loosens his tongue; nothing else does.
speech: Casual, short answers, deadpan jokes when he's comfortable.
hardFacts: I drive the cab out of the rank near the crossing.
I've had this route for six years.
I know every alley shortcut in the Hook.
I don't ask passengers questions.
I keep a jar of coins by the seat for the phone box at the crossing, in case a fare needs to make a call I didn't hear.

secret.line: I run quiet late-night deliveries for cash under the seat, no questions asked.

need: A mechanic's favor to keep his cab running through the winter.
lines: Where to. And no, I'm not going up Copper Row at this hour, not for double.
Two and six. Same as it was last night, and you were surprised then and all.
I've a very poor memory for faces. Costs extra to make it worse.

name: Luka
summary: Runs a repair cart fixing locks, latches, and window frames for half the Hook, having lost his corner shop to bad rent two years back. Keeps a tin box of spare keys for his regulars, sorted by address.
personality: Methodical and quiet, more comfortable with tools in his hands than words in his mouth, but reliable to a fault once he's taken your coin.
speech: Talks in short, practical sentences, often mid-task, rarely finishing one thought before starting the next job.
hardFacts: I've fixed locks for half the buildings on this street.
I keep spare keys for regulars in a tin box, labeled by address.
I lost my shop on the corner two years back to bad rent, work from a cart now.
I don't ask what a key's for if the coin's good.
I take messages for jobs at the bar since I've no phone of my own, Rocco writes them on a slip and I settle up with him in coin at the end of the week.

secret.line: I cut a duplicate key for anyone who pays, no questions asked, and I don't log those.

need: Steady paying clients and protection from a rival repairman undercutting his prices
lines: This latch, it's the pin, see— hang on, your window frame's swollen too, I'll need the plane for that.
Two quid for the lock, another one if you want it before Friday— who's next, Mrs. Odell? Tell her I'm running late.
Not this key, that one— the brass one, it's for the Hendersons, everyone wants their spare cut same day.

name: Nada
summary: Runs the communal laundry, washing linens for half the tenements and seeing every stain, tear, and unexplained absence that passes through her tubs. Eighteen years in the same spot has made her a quiet archive of the district's small disasters.
personality: Warm-faced and gossip-proof in public, but she keeps a mental ledger of who's been careless lately, and nothing much rattles her anymore.
speech: Speaks plainly, punctuates sentences with sighs, calls everyone 'love' regardless of age.
hardFacts: I've run the laundry on this corner for eighteen years.
I know whose sheets don't come home for washing anymore.
I found blood on a coat once and said nothing about it.
I close up by dusk, never later.
I keep the tab book by the till, and if a man's short he leaves his watch or his word, and I write down which one it was.

secret.line: I skim a little off the wash money and report lower earnings to the building's owner.

need: Someone to lean on a client who's stopped paying his laundry tab
lines: Oh, love, that collar's not coming out, not if the Pope himself prayed over it.
Three weeks now he's owed me, love. Three weeks. I don't chase, I just... remember.
Blood's easy, love, it's the wine that never lifts. Sighs. Sit down, you look worse than the sheets.

name: Ante
summary: Processes paperwork at the customs shed and knows exactly which manifests get a second look and which slide through. A debt on the docks has him looking for extra income he'd rather not explain.
personality: Nervous and precise, terrified of losing his post, but greed keeps pulling him toward small favors he swears are the last one.
speech: Fast talker who over-explains, laughs a little too much when he's uncomfortable.
hardFacts: I stamp manifests at the customs shed six days a week.
I can tell you which crates get inspected before they're even unloaded.
I owe money to a man on the docks I'd rather not name.
I've backdated a form or two for the right price.
I settle up my tab at the corner shop every other Friday, cash in the envelope same as my wages, and I've never once let it run past the second week.

secret.line: I take bribes to wave certain crates through the shed uninspected.

need: Money to settle a dockside debt before it becomes someone else's problem
lines: It's stamped, it's fine, it's. Look, I wouldn't put my name on it if it wasn't fine, right, ha, it's fine.
Two manifests, that's all, I just. I don't even read the second one that close, honestly, who has the time.
You want it back Thursday? Thursday's tight but, no, no, Thursday's good, ha, Thursday works.

name: Pero
summary: Pero cuts and repairs keys from a cramped stall near the pawnshop, quietly duplicating sets for regulars who pay a little extra. He's outlived two marriages and now lives alone above his shop, precise about everything except his own comfort.
personality: Methodical and soft-spoken, he treats every key like a small puzzle worth solving properly. He's not greedy in the loud way, just quietly willing to bend rules for steady coin.
speech: Short, clipped sentences, often about tolerances and fit, rarely wastes a word on feeling.
hardFacts: I've run the key stall by the pawnshop for nineteen years.
I keep a ledger of every key I've ever cut, going back a decade.
I sharpened the shears for Marek's bar every autumn until he died.
I've never worked north of the crossing.
I take messages for the shop through Rocco at the bar door since I've no phone of my own up here.

secret.line: I cut a duplicate key for a man I'm fairly sure fences stolen goods, and I never asked why he needed it.

need: Wants steady, trustworthy buyers for his lock work instead of one-off strangers he can't vouch for.
lines: Off by half a millimeter. That's the whole problem right there.
Come back Thursday. Not before.
Cut it once, cut it right. I don't do twice.

name: Zeljko
summary: Zeljko sells tickets at the ferry stop and watches the harbor traffic more closely than anyone realizes. He's jumpy by nature, always half-expecting to be caught at something, even when he hasn't done anything yet.
personality: Nervous and eager to please, he avoids confrontation at almost any cost. He notices patterns in people the way others notice weather.
speech: Talks quickly and apologetically, often trailing off mid-sentence when he thinks he's said too much.
hardFacts: I've sold ferry tickets at the stop for six years.
I know the ferry schedule better than the captain does.
I saw the warehouse smoke the night it burned, from across the water.
I never take the late shift anymore.

I keep the till receipts in a biscuit tin under the counter because the harbor office won't fix the drawer lock, and I count them twice before I walk them to the office phone box to call in the day's take.

secret.line: I skim small change from the ticket till most days and tell myself it doesn't count.

need: Wants someone to quietly cover for him if the till ever comes up short during an audit.
lines: I didn't see anything, I mean, I saw him, but I wasn't looking, you know, I just happened to—sorry, forget it.
The four-fifteen was late again, not that it matters, not that anyone asked me, I just, I noticed, that's all.
You want a ticket or— sorry, sorry, here, I'll just, here.

name: Mila
summary: Mila runs a small laundry near the boarding house, washing linens for half the district and hearing everything through wet sheets and doorway gossip. She's fiercely loyal to anyone who's ever been decent to her.
personality: Warm and steady, she keeps other people's secrets the way she keeps their linens, folded neatly and never mentioned. Underneath the calm she's protective to the point of stubbornness.
speech: Speaks plainly and warmly, often folding practical advice into small talk about stains and weather.
hardFacts: I've done the boarding house's laundry for four years.
I found a bloodstained shirt in a batch once and said nothing to anyone.
I know whose sheets never get washed because they're never home.
I grew up in tenement_south.
I take messages for half the boarding house on the payphone in my hallway, there's a jar by it for the coppers

secret.line: I still have that bloodstained shirt hidden in my back room, never returned or reported.

need: Wants protection from a customer who's started following her home after closing.
lines: Blood'll set if you use hot water, cold water and salt, that's the trick
Rain's coming in by evening, best get that washing off the line by four
You leave it with me Tuesday, I'll have it back to you Thursday, no bother

name: Karlo
summary: Karlo has stamped forms at the customs shed for over two decades, deciding which crates get flagged and which pass quietly through. He owes money he won't discuss, and it shapes every choice he makes lately.
personality: Outwardly gruff and businesslike, he's grown comfortable looking the other way for the right price. Loyalty comes second to whatever keeps him solvent this week.
speech: Brisk and transactional, he talks in terms of paperwork and percentages even when the subject is personal.
hardFacts: I've stamped customs forms at the shed for twenty-two years.
I can flag or clear any crate that passes through here.
I was questioned about the warehouse fire but cleared of anything.
I owe money to a man I won't name.
I take messages at the customs shed's one phone line, and if a man rings twice before noon I know to expect him at the side door by six.

secret.line: I take bribes to wave certain crates through without inspection, and I've stopped counting how many.

need: Wants a quiet way to pay off his debt before whoever he owes decides to collect it differently.
lines: Call it a processing fee, ten percent, and the crate never existed.
You want it stamped today or stamped correctly, pick one.
I don't ask what's inside. I ask what it's worth to keep it that way.

name: Drazen
summary: Drazen fixes engines and locks at the repair yard, and can cut a key or crack a cheap padlock faster than most people can find their wallet. He's quiet about who asks him for what.
personality: Methodical and unbothered, he treats every job the same whether it's a stuck carburetor or a stuck door. He doesn't gossip, but he remembers favors owed with the precision of a ledger.
speech: Short, technical sentences, often trailing off mid-thought while his hands keep working.
hardFacts: I've run the repair yard since Marek's time, before that even.
I can cut a working key from a wax impression in under an hour.
I owe Rocco for vouching for me when I first got here.
I don't touch anything with the harbor office's seal on it.
I keep the yard's only phone by the compressor and charge a coin a call, mostly for the dock lads whose landlords won't run a line up.

secret.line: I've cut duplicate keys for three different warehouse locks over the years and never logged who asked.

need: Steady, quiet work that doesn't draw customs attention.
lines: Carbon's built up in the... yeah. Give it a minute.
Not the tumbler, the spring behind it. Always the spring.
Tell him Thursday. If he asks twice, tell him Friday.

name: Nevenka
summary: Nevenka runs the wash lines at the laundry, handling the clothes and linens of half the Hook, which means she notices bloodstains, torn pockets, and things people forget to check before dropping off a bundle. She's careful never to say what she's seen.
personality: Tired but sharp-eyed, she keeps her head down and her opinions to herself out of long habit. She's protective of her son and will bend rules quietly to keep him out of trouble.
speech: Soft-voiced, apologetic phrasing, often starting sentences with 'I only mean to say-'.
hardFacts: I've worked the laundry on the corner near the crossing for eighteen years.
My son owes money to men I won't name.
I found a torn, bloodied shirt in a delivery bag last month and said nothing.
I know whose sheets smell like the docks and whose smell like the chapel.
I keep a tally book by the till for the ones who pay Friday against what they dropped off Monday, and half the Hook's wages come to me in an envelope before they come to the rent.

secret.line: I've been quietly pawning small items left in pockets to cover my son's debts.

need: Money to settle her son's debt before it becomes someone else's problem.
lines: I only mean to say- that shirt come in with a tear already, I didn't do that.
I only mean to say, if someone was asking, I never saw the collar, not really saw it.
I only mean to say- you didn't hear the machines were down Tuesday, from me you didn't.

name: Tibor
summary: Tibor has run the repair yard on warehouse row for eleven years, fixing locks, hinges, and anything with a latch. He keeps his head down and his hands steady, which is why people trust him with things they'd rather not explain.
personality: Quiet and methodical, he measures twice before saying anything at all. He's not brave, but he's reliable, and that counts for more on the Row.
speech: Speaks in short, practical sentences, often trailing off mid-thought while his hands keep working.
hardFacts: I've run the repair yard on the Row for eleven years.
I can cut a copy of nearly any key if you bring me the original for an hour.
I taught myself to pick simple locks fixing jammed doors.
I don't ask why someone needs two extra keys made.
I keep a wage tin under the bench, and if a man comes in with no coin I let him run a tab chalked on the inside of the shutter.

secret.line: I've sold spare keys to Sam's contacts for petty jobs without telling the owners.

need: wants steady scrap metal and parts supply, or someone to smooth things over if customs starts checking his tool permits
lines: Latch is bent, not broke. Give it a day.
Depends what you need it to forget how to lock, and...
I don't ask what's behind the door. Just the door.

name: Irena
summary: Irena has scrubbed the Hook district's linens for six years, learning more from stains than most people learn from gossip. She's careful with what she notices and even more careful about what she says out loud.
personality: Warm on the surface but privately anxious about money, she smiles easily while calculating rent in her head. She's not greedy so much as scared of falling behind again.
speech: Chatty and familiar with regulars, but her voice tightens whenever the subject turns to money.
hardFacts: I've worked the laundry behind the bathhouse for six years.
I know whose sheets and shirts come in with blood or grease stains.
I keep a ledger of who pays late and who pays in coin versus notes.
I can get stains out that shouldn't be got out, for the right price.

I take the rent envelope round to the landlord's agent myself on Friday nights because he's never once had a phone connected, and I keep my own tally of who owes what in a rent book under the counter.

secret.line: I skim a little starch and soap to sell on the side to cover rent.

need: needs someone to vouch for her with the landlord, or steady clients who pay on time
lines: Oh, that's Mrs. Feld's tablecloth, always with the wine, bless her - now the collars, love, are we squaring up today or Friday?
Same as last week, same as the week before, I don't mind carrying it a few days but it does add up on my end, you know how it is
Go on then, tell me about the wedding - just, before you do, did you want to settle the eleven pounds or shall I write it down again?
